On the first Monday of every month, the city sold what it had found on the buses. The sale took place in a low brick building behind the depot, where the windows were too high to see through and the coffee came out of a machine that gave you a wooden stirrer whether you wanted one or not. I went because my father had left his umbrella on the number six. It was a black umbrella with a duck’s head for a handle. He’d been dead nine months, which meant it had been missing for at least nine months and a day.

The woman at the desk asked whether I had reported it missing. I said I hadn’t known it was missing until I cleared out his hallway. She turned her monitor so I could see the form. There was a field for the date of loss, and another for the approximate time. Neither accepted a dash. We tried leaving them blank. The computer outlined both fields in red. Finally she entered noon on the day I’d cleared the hallway. “That’s the day you lost it,” she said. I had been ready to dislike her, but this struck me as fair.

There were thirty-seven umbrellas in the sale, bundled in threes with masking tape. None had a duck’s head. I bought a bundle anyway. Outside, I opened the first umbrella and discovered it was meant for a child: yellow, with two fabric ears that stood up when the canopy opened. The second had a broken rib. The third was a promotional umbrella from a dentist’s office and said *OPEN WIDE* across two panels. This one worked. I stood beneath it in the depot yard, holding the other two, while a bus reversed into a bay with the slow, emphatic beeping of an appliance asking to be unplugged.

My father had driven a bus before I was born. I knew this from a photograph, not from him. In the photograph he was leaning out of the driver’s window in shirtsleeves, laughing at something beyond the frame. The bus was cream and green. When I asked him, once, what had been so funny, he told me the bus wasn’t supposed to be green. The city had ordered blue paint and someone had sent green, and by the time anyone noticed, they had done eleven buses. I asked what that had to do with the photograph. He looked at it again. “Nothing,” he said.

At the next sale I bought a lunchbox containing a fork and a small saltshaker. In June I bought a red scarf. The woman at the desk, whose name was Val, began putting the umbrellas aside so I could look at them before she taped them together. She didn’t ask about my father. She did ask if I wanted to know what happened to the things they couldn’t sell. I said I assumed they went to charity. “Most do,” she said, and opened a bottom drawer. Inside were seven single shoes. She shut it again. I had the sense she had meant to explain them and then thought better of it.

In July a man came in looking for a hearing aid. He said it was in a blue case and he’d lost it on the number six. Val brought out two blue cases. He opened the first and said it wasn’t his. He opened the second and said it wasn’t his either. Then he picked up the first one again, took out the hearing aid, and put it in his ear. Val asked him something. “Excuse me?” he said. She asked him again, louder this time. He took it out and looked at it with an expression of genuine annoyance. “Yes,” he said. “That’s definitely mine.”

That afternoon I took the six all the way to the end of the line. It terminated beside a supermarket. The driver switched off the engine, came down the aisle, and said she’d be going back in twelve minutes if that was what I was waiting for. I asked if she found many umbrellas. “Not as many as you’d think,” she said. People forgot them on mornings when it rained and cleared up. If it was still raining when they got off, they remembered. I thought of all the sunny afternoons on which my father might have walked home empty-handed, pleased to find the weather had improved.

In August there was a black umbrella with a carved wooden handle. It was a horse. Val set it on the desk between us, and I ran my thumb over its ears. On the underside of the handle someone had stuck a strip of white tape with a phone number written on it. We dialed from the desk. A young man answered. When I explained, he said, “Oh, he’ll be so embarrassed.” Then he asked if we could hold it until Friday. I said yes, although I didn’t work there and had no idea whether we could. Val took a tag from a drawer and wrote *FRIDAY* on it.

I had brought a picture of the duck umbrella to show her. It was a photograph of my father at a cousin’s wedding, taken just outside the reception hall. Someone inside must have called his name. He was half turned away, reaching for the door with his left hand, holding the closed umbrella in his right. Val looked at the picture for a long time. “Those doors were a nuisance,” she said. “You had to lift them by the handle or they’d catch.” It turned out she’d been married in the same hall. I’d been there twice and hadn’t noticed anything about the doors.

I stopped going to the sales after that summer. I still have the dentist’s umbrella. Last week, on the six, I saw a woman get up and leave a yellow umbrella on the seat beside her. I called out, and she turned, but she didn’t come back for it. She pointed through the window. We’d been underground by the station, and neither of us had noticed that it had stopped raining. I carried it down to her anyway. At the curb she pressed the button to make sure it was hers. Two small ears sprang up, and we both laughed.
